Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

issues.explanation: The trigger set is mostly coherent with rape trauma (locked/confined spaces, sexual-violence comments), but sirens are hard to connect to the rest of this profile and trauma context. With strong Negative Appraisals↔Threat and links from both to Triggers, the triggers should plausibly cue the patient's threat meanings; sirens do not fit the sexual-assault/confinement theme represented by the other trigger and appraisal items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilant unsafe-world items (back to wall, staying alert to sleep) fit well, but 'taking too many risks' pulls in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile with the same immediate threat style. It also lacks support elsewhere in the profile, since no other items suggest disinhibition, anger, numbing, or self-destructive coping.

vignette: Kwame sat on the edge of the examination table in Dr. Evans' office, his hands resting flat on his knees, palms pressed hard against his skin. Six months ago, the atmosphere in a closed room had shifted in an instant. He had gone to a colleague's office to discuss a collaborative research grant, trusting the man's professional reputation. He remembered the heavy oak door clicking shut behind him, the way the afternoon light narrowed into slats across the carpet, and the sudden, violent realization that his body was no longer his own. He had been raped in that locked room, stripped of his agency while the door remained shut. He had not fought. He had gone rigid, tracking every movement in the space, calculating exits that the lock had sealed off. When the door finally opened, he had walked out with his shoulders hunched forward, already bracing for the next strike. The weeks that followed did not bring clarity. They brought a quiet reshaping of his daily terrain. In his role as a psychologist at the university counseling center, Kwame began pushing his desk against the perimeter wall, pressing his back flush against the painted brick. He could not sit in the center of the room; the open space behind him felt like a gap he had to fill with solid structure. When male graduate students knocked to discuss clinical rotations, he found himself canceling appointments or routing them through his department chair instead. He told himself it was about scheduling efficiency, but the truth sat heavier in his chest. Being alone with men now carried a low, constant hum in his ears, a physical alertness that made his jaw clench until his teeth ached. He stopped lingering in the staff lounge when colleagues began debating recent campus sexual violence statistics. The comments felt sharp and immediate, pulling him back to the heavy door and the suffocating quiet of that room. He did not leave the lounge; he simply stood there, listening to the murmur, his body already taut, already scanning for exits that weren't there. Sleep offered no respite. Kwame lay awake long past midnight, the ceiling above him a blank canvas he refused to look at. He needed to stay alert, convinced that drifting off would leave him unprepared for whatever might happen next. He did not know what next would be, but the uncertainty itself was a weight he refused to set down. Even during the day, when he knew he was behind his own deadbolts at home, his muscles refused to yield. He would pace the kitchen, check the lock three times, and then stand by the window, watching the streetlights flicker on. What frightened him most was not just the fear of another attack, but the conviction that he was fundamentally unable to stop bad things from finding him. He felt transparent to his colleagues, as though the violation lived just beneath his skin, visible to them simply by looking at him. He had come to believe there was no future worth building, only a series of rooms he would have to navigate carefully, doors he would have to monitor, and men he would have to keep at a distance. The tipping point arrived on a Tuesday when a train car stalled between stations. The emergency lights buzzed overhead, and the carriage fell silent except for the sharp intakes of breath from passengers checking their phones. Kwame pressed himself into the corner, his back against the cold metal wall, his breath coming in short, controlled gasps. He realized he could no longer sustain the careful architecture he had built. He had requested a referral through his hospital's employee assistance program, and now he sat in a private practice office, his hands resting on his knees, palms down. He was hoping someone could help him understand why his own mind had become a perimeter he could not leave. He was most afraid that the door would click shut again, that he would be trapped once more, and that he would never feel safe in his own life. But beneath the fear, there was a quiet, stubborn determination to stop living in anticipation of a lock that might never turn again.
